claim: Long-lived cells such as terminally differentiated postmitotic neurons and glia must cope with the accumulation of damage over the course of an animal's lifespan.
source: Long-lived cells such as terminally differentiated postmitotic neurons and glia must cope with the accumulation of damage over the course of an animal's lifespan.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular biology that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: How long-lived cells deal with ageing-related damage is poorly understood.
source: How long-lived cells deal with ageing-related damage is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Polyploid cells accumulate in the adult fly brain.
source: Here we show that polyploid cells accumulate in the adult fly brain and that polyploidy protects against DNA damage-induced cell death.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data and imaging presented in the manuscript.

claim: Polyploidy protects against DNA damage-induced cell death.
source: Here we show that polyploid cells accumulate in the adult fly brain and that polyploidy protects against DNA damage-induced cell death.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing differential cell death rates between diploid and polyploid cells.

claim: Multiple types of neurons and glia that are diploid at eclosion become polyploid in the adult Drosophila brain.
source: Multiple types of neurons and glia that are diploid at eclosion, become polyploid in the adult Drosophila brain.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using cell-type specific GAL4 drivers shown in Figure 2.

claim: The optic lobes exhibit the highest levels of polyploidy.
source: The optic lobes exhibit the highest levels of polyploidy, associated with an elevated DNA damage response in this brain region.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing different brain regions shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The optic lobes are associated with an elevated DNA damage response.
source: The optic lobes exhibit the highest levels of polyploidy, associated with an elevated DNA damage response in this brain region.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and pH2AV immunostaining shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inducing oxidative stress leads to an earlier onset of polyploidy.
source: Inducing oxidative stress or exogenous DNA damage leads to an earlier onset of polyploidy, and polyploid cells in the adult brain are more resistant to DNA damage-induced cell death than diploid cells.
evidence: This is supported by paraquat treatment experiments shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Inducing exogenous DNA damage leads to an earlier onset of polyploidy.
source: Inducing oxidative stress or exogenous DNA damage leads to an earlier onset of polyploidy, and polyploid cells in the adult brain are more resistant to DNA damage-induced cell death than diploid cells.
evidence: This is supported by UV treatment experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Polyploid cells in the adult brain are more resistant to DNA damage-induced cell death than diploid cells.
source: Inducing oxidative stress or exogenous DNA damage leads to an earlier onset of polyploidy, and polyploid cells in the adult brain are more resistant to DNA damage-induced cell death than diploid cells.
evidence: This is supported by propidium iodide incorporation data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: Polyploidy may serve a protective role for neurons and glia in adult Drosophila melanogaster brains.
source: Our results suggest polyploidy may serve a protective role for neurons and glia in adult Drosophila melanogaster brains.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The adult central nervous system of Drosophila melanogaster comprises ~110,000 cells.
source: The adult central nervous system of Drosophila melanogaster comprises ~110,000 cells, most of which are generated in the larval and early pupal stages of development from various progenitor cell types (Truman and Bate, 1988; White and Kankel, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most cells in the adult Drosophila CNS are generated in the larval and early pupal stages of development from various progenitor cell types.
source: The adult central nervous system of Drosophila melanogaster comprises ~110,000 cells, most of which are generated in the larval and early pupal stages of development from various progenitor cell types (Truman and Bate, 1988; White and Kankel, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By late metamorphosis, the Drosophila pupal brain is normally completely non-cycling and negative for markers of proliferation such as thymidine analog incorporation and mitotic markers.
source: By late metamorphosis, the Drosophila pupal brain is normally completely non-cycling and negative for markers of proliferation such as thymidine analog incorporation and mitotic markers (Awasaki et al., 2008; Pahl et al., 2019; Siegrist et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Very little neurogenesis and gliogenesis are normally observed in the adult Drosophila brain.
source: In the adult, very little neurogenesis and gliogenesis are normally observed (Awasaki et al., 2008; Ito and Hotta, 1992; von Trotha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A population of about 40 adult neural progenitors has been reported in the optic lobe.
source: A population of about 40 adult neural progenitors has been reported in the optic lobe and a population of glial progenitors has been reported in the central brain (Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A population of glial progenitors has been reported in the central brain.
source: A population of about 40 adult neural progenitors has been reported in the optic lobe and a population of glial progenitors has been reported in the central brain (Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon damage or cell loss, hallmarks of cycling have been shown to be activated in the adult brain.
source: Upon damage or cell loss, hallmarks of cycling have been shown to be activated, although the overall level of proliferation in the adult brain remains very low (Crocker et al., 2020; Fernandez-Hernandez et al., 2019; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The overall level of proliferation in the adult brain remains very low.
source: Upon damage or cell loss, hallmarks of cycling have been shown to be activated, although the overall level of proliferation in the adult brain remains very low (Crocker et al., 2020; Fernandez-Hernandez et al., 2019; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The brain of the adult fly is thought to be almost entirely postmitotic with most cells in G0 with a diploid (2C) DNA content.
source: Thus, the brain of the adult fly is thought to be almost entirely postmitotic with most cells in G0 with a diploid (2C) DNA content.
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cells that constitute the 'blood-brain barrier' of Drosophila are a known exception to the diploid state of adult brain cells.
source: One known exception to this are the cells that constitute the 'blood-brain barrier' of Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference based on the context and subsequent description of SPG cells.

claim: The 'blood-brain barrier' in Drosophila is made up of specialised cells called the Sub-perineurial glia (SPGs).
source: The 'blood-brain barrier' in Drosophila is made up of specialised cells called the Sub-perineurial glia (SPGs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila anatomy.

claim: SPGs employ variant cell cycles termed endocycles that involve DNA replication without karyokinesis or cytokinesis.
source: These cells are very few in number and achieve growth without cell division by employing variant cell cycles termed endocycles, that involve DNA replication without karyokinesis or cytokinesis, as well as endomitotic cycles that involve DNA replication and karyokinesis without cytokinesis (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPGs employ endomitotic cycles that involve DNA replication and karyokinesis without cytokinesis.
source: These cells are very few in number and achieve growth without cell division by employing variant cell cycles termed endocycles, that involve DNA replication without karyokinesis or cytokinesis, as well as endomitotic cycles that involve DNA replication and karyokinesis without cytokinesis (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The SPGs undergo variant cell cycles to increase their size rapidly to sustain the growth of the underlying brain during larval development.
source: The SPGs undergo these variant cell cycles to increase their size rapidly to sustain the growth of the underlying brain during larval development.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about SPG function.

claim: The polyploidization of SPGs plays an important role in maintaining their epithelial barrier function.
source: The polyploidization of these cells plays an important role in maintaining their epithelial barrier function, although it remains unclear whether these cells continue to endocycle or endomitose in the adult.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about SPG function.

claim: It remains unclear whether SPGs continue to endocycle or endomitose in the adult.
source: The polyploidization of these cells plays an important role in maintaining their epithelial barrier function, although it remains unclear whether these cells continue to endocycle or endomitose in the adult.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Polyploidy can confer an increased biosynthetic capacity to cells.
source: Polyploidy can also confer an increased biosynthetic capacity to cells and resistance to DNA damage induced cell death (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Lee et al., 2009; Mehrotra et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidy can confer resistance to DNA damage induced cell death.
source: Polyploidy can also confer an increased biosynthetic capacity to cells and resistance to DNA damage induced cell death (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Lee et al., 2009; Mehrotra et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several studies have noted neurons and glia in the adult fly brain with large nuclei.
source: Several studies have noted neurons and glia in the adult fly brain with large nuclei (Robinow and White, 1991; Winberg et al., 1992) and in some cases neurons and glia of other insect species in the adult CNS are known to be polyploid (Nordlander and Edwards, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons and glia of other insect species in the adult CNS are known to be polyploid.
source: Several studies have noted neurons and glia in the adult fly brain with large nuclei (Robinow and White, 1991; Winberg et al., 1992) and in some cases neurons and glia of other insect species in the adult CNS are known to be polyploid (Nordlander and Edwards, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rare instances of neuronal polyploidy have been reported in vertebrates under normal conditions.
source: Rare instances of neuronal polyploidy have been reported in vertebrates under normal conditions (Morillo et al., 2010) and even in the CNS of mammals (López-Sánchez and Frade, 2013; Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuronal polyploidy has been reported in the CNS of mammals.
source: Rare instances of neuronal polyploidy have been reported in vertebrates under normal conditions (Morillo et al., 2010) and even in the CNS of mammals (López-Sánchez and Frade, 2013; Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidization is employed in response to tissue damage and helps maintain organ size.
source: Polyploidization is employed in response to tissue damage and helps maintain organ size (Cohen et al., 2018; Tamori and Deng, 2013; Losick et al., 2016; Losick et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidy may be a strategy to deal with damage accumulated with age in the brain, a tissue with very limited cell division potential.
source: Therefore, polyploidy may be a strategy to deal with damage accumulated with age in the brain, a tissue with very limited cell division potential.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the context and previous findings.

claim: The proportion of polyploidy increases as the animals approach middle-age.
source: Here we show that polyploid cells accumulate in the adult fly brain and that this proportion of polyploidy increases as the animals approach middle-age.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Inducing oxidative stress can lead to increased levels of polyploidy.
source: We also observe increased DNA damage with age, and show that inducing oxidative stress and exogenous DNA damage can lead to increased levels of polyploidy.
evidence: This is supported by paraquat treatment data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: DNA damage increases with age in the Drosophila brain.
source: We also observe increased DNA damage with age, and show that inducing oxidative stress and exogenous DNA damage can lead to increased levels of polyploidy.
evidence: This is supported by pH2AV staining and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cell ploidy often scales with cell size and biosynthetic capacity.
source: Cell ploidy often scales with cell size and biosynthetic capacity (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Orr-Weaver, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The brain is thought to be a notable exception to the rule that ploidy scales with cell size.
source: The brain is thought to be a notable exception to this rule, where the size of postmitotic diploid neurons and glia can be highly variable.
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge in the field.

claim: The size of postmitotic diploid neurons and glia can be highly variable.
source: The brain is thought to be a notable exception to this rule, where the size of postmitotic diploid neurons and glia can be highly variable.
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cell proliferation and DNA replication ceases in the pupal brain after 24 hr into metamorphosis (24 hr APF) under normal culturing conditions.
source: Using this approach we confirmed that under normal culturing conditions, cell proliferation and DNA replication ceases in the pupal brain after 24 hr into metamorphosis (24 hr APF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), and that only the previously described mushroom body neuroblasts continue to replicate their DNA and divide in late pupa (Siegrist et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and citation to previous literature.

claim: Only the mushroom body neuroblasts continue to replicate their DNA and divide in late pupa.
source: Using this approach we confirmed that under normal culturing conditions, cell proliferation and DNA replication ceases in the pupal brain after 24 hr into metamorphosis (24 hr APF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), and that only the previously described mushroom body neuroblasts continue to replicate their DNA and divide in late pupa (Siegrist et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and citation to previous literature.

claim: The brains of newly eclosed adult flies are 98–99% diploid.
source: The brains of newly eclosed adult flies are 98–99% diploid and we, like others, only rarely observe EdU incorporation during the first week of adulthood in wild-type flies under normal conditions but not later in adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2009; Siegrist et al., 2010; von Trotha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: EdU incorporation is only rarely observed during the first week of adulthood in wild-type flies under normal conditions.
source: The brains of newly eclosed adult flies are 98–99% diploid and we, like others, only rarely observe EdU incorporation during the first week of adulthood in wild-type flies under normal conditions but not later in adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2009; Siegrist et al., 2010; von Trotha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and citations to previous literature.

claim: EdU incorporation is not observed later in adulthood in wild-type flies under normal conditions.
source: The brains of newly eclosed adult flies are 98–99% diploid and we, like others, only rarely observe EdU incorporation during the first week of adulthood in wild-type flies under normal conditions but not later in adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2009; Siegrist et al., 2010; von Trotha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and citations to previous literature.

claim: A distinct population of cells with DNA content of 4C and up to >16C appears in brains of aged animals of various genotypes under normal culture conditions.
source: We were therefore surprised to find a distinct population of cells with DNA content of 4C and up to >16C appearing in brains of aged animals of various genotypes under normal culture conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Polyploid cells appear as early as 7 days into adulthood.
source: Polyploid cells appear as early as 7 days into adulthood, and the proportion of polyploidy continues to rise until animals are 21 days old (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The proportion of polyploidy continues to rise until animals are 21 days old.
source: Polyploid cells appear as early as 7 days into adulthood, and the proportion of polyploidy continues to rise until animals are 21 days old (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in polyploidy is only observed until week 3, after which the proportion of polyploid cells observed remains variable from animal to animal but on average does not increase.
source: This increase in polyploidy is only observed until week 3, after which the proportion of polyploid cells observed remains variable from animal to animal, but on average, does not increase.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Similar patterns of polyploidy accumulation are observed in males and females.
source: We observe similar patterns of polyploidy accumulation in males and females (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Oregon-R flies show lower levels of polyploidy in the first two weeks than w1118 and Canton-S.
source: Interestingly, Oregon-R flies show lower levels of polyploidy in the first two weeks than w1118 and Canton-S suggesting that different genetic backgrounds may influence polyploidy in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Different genetic backgrounds may influence polyploidy in the brain.
source: Interestingly, Oregon-R flies show lower levels of polyploidy in the first two weeks than w1118 and Canton-S suggesting that different genetic backgrounds may influence polyploidy in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of different polyploidy levels in different strains.

claim: D.americana and D.mauritiana show accumulation of polyploidy.
source: While both species show accumulation of polyploidy, it is interesting to note that they show differences in levels of polyploidy.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: D.americana and D.mauritiana show differences in levels of polyploidy.
source: While both species show accumulation of polyploidy, it is interesting to note that they show differences in levels of polyploidy.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of the polyploid cells appear to be tetraploid.
source: The majority of the polyploid cells appear to be tetraploid, and the fraction of cells exhibiting >4C DNA content increases during the first week of adulthood, but remains relatively consistent with age.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The fraction of cells exhibiting >4C DNA content increases during the first week of adulthood but remains relatively consistent with age.
source: The majority of the polyploid cells appear to be tetraploid, and the fraction of cells exhibiting >4C DNA content increases during the first week of adulthood, but remains relatively consistent with age.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a low level of polyploidy in the central brain and VNC that increases with age.
source: We found that while there is a low level of polyploidy in the central brain and VNC that increases with age, most of the polyploidy comes from the optic lobes.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most of the polyploidy comes from the optic lobes.
source: We found that while there is a low level of polyploidy in the central brain and VNC that increases with age, most of the polyploidy comes from the optic lobes.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: By 3 weeks, over 20% of the cells in the optic lobes can exhibit polyploidy.
source: Strikingly, by 3 weeks, over 20% of the cells in the optic lobes can exhibit polyploidy.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Canton-S animals reared in complete darkness did not show difference in polyploidy compared to age-matched controls raised in regular 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycles.
source: Canton-S animals reared in complete darkness did not show difference in polyploidy compared to age-matched controls raised in regular 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: glass60j flies devoid of photoreceptors and pigment cells in compound eyes still show polyploidy.
source: However, glass60j flies devoid of photoreceptors and pigment cells in compound eyes (Helfrich-Förster et al., 2001) still show polyploidy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation to previous literature.

claim: The SPGs are highly polyploid.
source: When we used the SPG driver moody-GAL4, we found that the SPGs are highly polyploid (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012), but contributed to less than 5% the polyploid cells observed in mature adult brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C and citation to previous literature.

claim: SPGs contribute to less than 5% of the polyploid cells observed in mature adult brains.
source: When we used the SPG driver moody-GAL4, we found that the SPGs are highly polyploid (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012), but contributed to less than 5% the polyploid cells observed in mature adult brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: In 10 day old adult brains, tracheal cells comprise less than 3% of all polyploid cells.
source: Using the tracheal driver breathless-GAL4, we found that in 10 day old adult brains, tracheal cells comprise less than 3% of all polyploid cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: 90% of the polyploid cells observed in the brain arise from cell types not previously known to become polyploid.
source: Thus, 90% of the polyploid cells we observe in the brain arise from cell types not previously known to become polyploid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantification of SPG and tracheal cell contributions.

claim: The adult fly brain is thought to be composed almost entirely of neurons (90% of total population) and glia (10% of total population).
source: The adult fly brain is thought to be composed almost entirely of neurons (90% of total population) and glia (10% of total population).
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge about Drosophila brain composition.

claim: By two weeks ~ 5–6% of cells expressing nSyb-GAL4 show >2C DNA content.
source: We found that indeed, by two weeks ~ 5–6% of cells expressing nSyb-GAL4 show >2C DNA content.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By 2 weeks ~ 6–7% of glia become polyploid in the adult brain.
source: Similarly, we used the pan-glial driver Repo-GAL4 and found that by 2 weeks ~ 6–7% of glia also become polyploid in the adult brain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neurons outnumber glial cells in the fly brain.
source: Neurons outnumber glial cells in the fly brain, and we find that the relative proportions of polyploid cells reflect the total ratio of neurons vs. glia in the adult brain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge about Drosophila brain composition.

claim: The relative proportions of polyploid cells reflect the total ratio of neurons vs. glia in the adult brain.
source: Neurons outnumber glial cells in the fly brain, and we find that the relative proportions of polyploid cells reflect the total ratio of neurons vs. glia in the adult brain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most differentiated cell types assayed in the optic lobes show some level of polyploidy by one week of age.
source: Interestingly, we found that most differentiated cell types we assayed in the optic lobes show some level of polyploidy by one week of age.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Polyploidy arises in multiple neuronal and glial types that are initially diploid upon eclosion and become polyploid after terminal differentiation and specifically during adulthood.
source: We conclude that polyploidy arises in multiple neuronal and glial types that are initially diploid upon eclosion and become polyploid after terminal differentiation and specifically during adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Cells in the brain could become polyploid either by re-entering the cell cycle or by undergoing cell fusion.
source: We reasoned that cells in the brain could become polyploid either by re-entering the cell cycle or by undergoing cell fusion (Alvarez-Dolado and Martínez-Losa, 2011; Giordano-Santini et al., 2016; Grendler et al., 2019; Losick et al., 2013; Schoenfelder et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2018; Starnes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge and citations to previous literature.

claim: Very little cell fusion occurs in the adult OL, even with age.
source: We conclude that very little cell fusion occurs in the adult OL, even with age.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on CoinFLP labeling experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inducing 'flipping' in cells that are already polyploid results in a fraction of double labeled yellow cells.
source: Previous work with CoinFLP has shown that inducing 'flipping' in cells that are already polyploid results in a fraction of double labeled yellow cells (Bosch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Heterozygous CoinFLP brain cells that become polyploid by replicating their genome during adulthood will contain two or more copies of the CoinFLP transgene cassette.
source: We therefore reasoned that heterozygous CoinFLP brain cells that become polyploid by replicating their genome during adulthood will contain two or more copies of the CoinFLP transgene cassette.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the genetics of the CoinFLP system.

claim: When labeling is induced at one day before polyploidy occurs, no double-labeled cells are observed in the optic lobe.
source: When we induce an adult FLP at one day, before polyploidy occurs, we do not observe any double-labeled cells in the optic lobe (Figure 4B) but when we induce an adult FLP at 30 days post-eclosion, we observe several double labeled cells (Figure 4B') indicating that these cells have undergone genome replication and contain at least two heterozygous copies of the CoinFLP transgenic cassette.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When labeling is induced at 30 days post-eclosion, several double labeled cells are observed.
source: When we induce an adult FLP at one day, before polyploidy occurs, we do not observe any double-labeled cells in the optic lobe (Figure 4B) but when we induce an adult FLP at 30 days post-eclosion, we observe several double labeled cells (Figure 4B') indicating that these cells have undergone genome replication and contain at least two heterozygous copies of the CoinFLP transgenic cassette.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B'.

claim: Cells that show double-labeling in late-FLP experiments have undergone genome replication and contain at least two heterozygous copies of the CoinFLP transgenic cassette.
source: When we induce an adult FLP at one day, before polyploidy occurs, we do not observe any double-labeled cells in the optic lobe (Figure 4B) but when we induce an adult FLP at 30 days post-eclosion, we observe several double labeled cells (Figure 4B') indicating that these cells have undergone genome replication and contain at least two heterozygous copies of the CoinFLP transgenic cassette.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CoinFLP labeling results.

claim: Around 300 double-labeled cells per optic lobes are observed in 14 day old brains using an adult 'late-FLP'.
source: To quantify this, we used an adult 'late-FLP' to drive nuclear GFP and RFP, and we observe around 300 double-labeled cells per optic lobes in 14 day old brains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of double-labelled nuclei in aged optic lobes suggest cells become polyploid by cell cycle re-entry and endoreduplicating DNA.
source: The presence of double-labelled nuclei in aged optic lobes suggest cells become polyploid by cell cycle re-entry and endoreduplicating DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CoinFLP labeling results.

claim: All CoinFLP double-labeled cells were confirmed to be polyploid by DAPI integrated intensity measurements.
source: All CoinFLP double-labeled cells were confirmed to be polyploid by DAPI integrated intensity measurements and 97% of all double-labeled cells show >2C DNA content by FACS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 97% of all CoinFLP double-labeled cells show >2C DNA content by FACS.
source: All CoinFLP double-labeled cells were confirmed to be polyploid by DAPI integrated intensity measurements and 97% of all double-labeled cells show >2C DNA content by FACS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: CoinFLP double-labeling confirmed several types of glia identifiable by location and shape to become polyploid, such as a subset of cortex glia of the outer and inner optic chiasm and astrocyte-like glia in the medulla of the OL.
source: CoinFLP double-labeling confirmed several types of glia identifiable by location and shape to become polyploid, such as a subset of cortex glia of the outer (Figure 4D) and inner (Figure 4E) optic chiasm and astrocyte-like glia (Figure 4F) in the medulla of the OL.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D,E,F.

claim: Expressing cdc6 RNAi in differentiated neurons using nSyb-GAL4 significantly reduced levels of polyploidy by 14d.
source: Using nSyb-GAL4, we expressed UAS-cdc6RNAi in differentiated neurons which significantly reduced levels of polyploidy by 14d (Figure 4G) from ~25% in control optic lobes to ~14% on optic lobes expressing the RNAi.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Knocking down geminin increases levels of polyploidy in the optic lobes.
source: We next knocked down geminin and found that we increase levels of polyploidy in the optic lobes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A fraction of post-mitotic neurons reactivate DNA replication to become polyploid in the adult fly brain.
source: This suggests that a fraction of post-mitotic neurons reactivate DNA replication to become polyploid in the adult fly brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc6 and geminin knockdown experiments.

claim: The most significant changes observed in the optic lobes at 21d compared to 2d include upregulation of genes associated with the cell cycle, DNA damage response and DNA damage repair.
source: The most significant changes observed in the optic lobes at 21d compared to 2d are shown in Figure 5A,B. Among the most significantly upregulated groups of genes are those associated with the cell cycle, DNA damage response and DNA damage repair.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The enrichment of up-regulated genes associated with the DNA damage response was also observed in the optic lobes at 7 days.
source: The enrichment of up-regulated genes associated with the DNA damage response was also observed in the optic lobes at 7 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but the enrichment and fold-induction of specific genes is stronger at day 21 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment and fold-induction of specific DNA damage response genes is stronger at day 21 than at day 7.
source: The enrichment of up-regulated genes associated with the DNA damage response was also observed in the optic lobes at 7 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but the enrichment and fold-induction of specific genes is stronger at day 21 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A gene expression signature associated with DNA damage is specific to the optic lobes.
source: A gene expression signature associated with DNA damage is specific to the optic lobes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data comparing different brain regions.

claim: The most significantly downregulated GO terms in the optic lobes at 21d are shared with the central brain and VNC and include metabolism, transmembrane transport and cellular respiration-associated processes.
source: However, the most significantly downregulated GO terms in the optic lobes at 21d are shared with the central brain and VNC and include metabolism, transmembrane transport and cellular respiration-associated processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Young brains show very low levels of pH2AV in both the optic lobes and central brain.
source: Young brains show very low levels of pH2AV in both the optic lobes and central brain (Figure 5C,C',E) but older brains show higher levels of pH2AV in the optic lobes compared to the central brain (Figure 5D,D',E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C,C',E.

claim: Older brains show higher levels of pH2AV in the optic lobes compared to the central brain.
source: Young brains show very low levels of pH2AV in both the optic lobes and central brain (Figure 5C,C',E) but older brains show higher levels of pH2AV in the optic lobes compared to the central brain (Figure 5D,D',E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D,D',E.

claim: Recent work has identified a specific transcriptional response to induced DNA damage in the head that involved a non-canonical role for tumor suppressor protein p53.
source: Recent work has identified a specific transcriptional response to induced DNA damage in the head that involved a non-canonical role for tumor suppressor protein p53 (Kurtz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Robust upregulation of hRIPD genes Ku80, Irbp, Cht8, CG3344 and CG4734 is observed in the RNAseq data set at 7d and 21d in optic lobes.
source: In addition to genes such as FANCI, loki, rad50 and xrp1 which are involved in a canonical, ionising radiation-induced DNA damage response, we also find robust upregulation of hRIPD genes Ku80, Irbp, Cht8, CG3344 and CG4734 in our RNAseq data set at 7d and 21d in optic lobes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: hRIPD genes are not as strongly upregulated in the aged central brain or VNC.
source: However, these genes are not as strongly upregulated in the aged central brain or VNC and p53 itself shows only a small increase in the optic lobes at 21d (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: p53 itself shows only a small increase in the optic lobes at 21d.
source: However, these genes are not as strongly upregulated in the aged central brain or VNC and p53 itself shows only a small increase in the optic lobes at 21d (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Upregulation of cell cycle genes such as myc, cyclin D, orc1 is observed specifically in the optic lobes and increases with age.
source: Consistent with cell cycle re-entry in a fraction of cells in the OL, upregulation of cell cycle genes such as myc, cyclin D, orc1 is observed specifically in the optic lobes and increases with age.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Polyploid cells in the salivary gland can tolerate high levels of DNA double-strand breaks and resist apoptosis caused by DNA damage.
source: Work in other polyploid tissues in Drosophila has shown that polyploid cells in the salivary gland can tolerate high levels of DNA double-strand breaks and resist apoptosis caused by DNA damage (Hassel et al., 2014; Mehrotra et al., 2008; Qi and Calvi, 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploid cells in tissues such as the salivary gland have intrinsically low levels of p53 protein and also suppress the expression of pro-apoptotic genes.
source: This is possible because polyploid cells in tissues such as the salivary gland have intrinsically low levels of p53 protein and also suppress the expression of pro-apoptotic genes (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DNA damage can induce polyploidization in various tissues and organisms.
source: It has also been shown in various tissues and organisms that DNA damage can induce polyploidization (Bretscher and Fox, 2016; Donovan and Corbo, 2012; Grendler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype or dominant-negative p53 in neurons did not result in a significant difference in levels of polyploidy in 7 day old brains.
source: To address this, we overexpressed wildtype (p53WT) or a dominant-negative allele of p53 (p53DN) that is unable to bind to DNA and evoke a transcriptional response in neurons using the nSyb-GAL4 driver (Figure 6A). We did not see a significant difference in levels of polyploidy in 7 day old brains with overexpression of either WT or mutant p53, suggesting that accumulation of polyploidy in neurons is p53-independent.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Accumulation of polyploidy in neurons is p53-independent.
source: To address this, we overexpressed wildtype (p53WT) or a dominant-negative allele of p53 (p53DN) that is unable to bind to DNA and evoke a transcriptional response in neurons using the nSyb-GAL4 driver (Figure 6A). We did not see a significant difference in levels of polyploidy in 7 day old brains with overexpression of either WT or mutant p53, suggesting that accumulation of polyploidy in neurons is p53-independent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the p53 overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of dead cells in overexpression of p53WT or p53DN conditions compared to control.
source: We did not see a significant difference in the proportion of dead cells in overexpression of p53WT or p53DN conditions compared to control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) consistent with recent work suggesting a non-canonical, non-apoptotic role for p53 in the adult Drosophila brain (Kurtz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cell death measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous literature.

claim: w1118 males treated with 2 mM paraquat from day of eclosion exhibit higher levels of polyploidy at 7 days compared to control w1118 males.
source: w1118 flies treated with low dose of 2 mM PQ from eclosion show increased DNA damage as well as increased polyploidy at 7d −14d (Figure 6B,D) but not increased cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: w1118 flies treated with 2 mM paraquat from eclosion show increased DNA damage.
source: w1118 flies treated with low dose of 2 mM PQ from eclosion show increased DNA damage as well as increased polyploidy at 7d −14d (Figure 6B,D) but not increased cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pH2AV staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: w1118 flies treated with 2 mM paraquat from eclosion do not show increased cell death.
source: w1118 flies treated with low dose of 2 mM PQ from eclosion show increased DNA damage as well as increased polyploidy at 7d −14d (Figure 6B,D) but not increased cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Flies treated with 900mJ of UV radiation at 2 days post-eclosion show significantly increased levels of polyploidy at day seven compared to mock-treated controls.
source: We treated flies with 900mJ of UV radiation by placing flies in a UV Stratalinker at 2 days post-eclosion (Grendler et al., 2019; Kang and Bashirullah, 2014) and observed significantly increased levels of polyploidy at day seven in UV-treated flies compared to mock-treated controls (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C and citations to previous literature.

claim: An acute increase in cell death is observed 16 hr post-exposure to UV.
source: We measured cell death using propidium-iodide (PI) incorporation (Grushko and Buttitta, 2015) and observed an acute increase in cell death 16 hr post-exposure to UV (Figure 6E), but no difference in cell death 5 days post-exposure.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6E and citation to previous literature.

claim: There is no difference in cell death 5 days post-exposure to UV.
source: We measured cell death using propidium-iodide (PI) incorporation (Grushko and Buttitta, 2015) and observed an acute increase in cell death 16 hr post-exposure to UV (Figure 6E), but no difference in cell death 5 days post-exposure.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cell death precedes accumulation of polyploidy upon induction of exogenous DNA damage.
source: This suggests that cell death precedes accumulation of polyploidy upon induction of exogenous DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal relationship between cell death and polyploidy accumulation after UV treatment.

claim: Newly eclosed flies exhibit a low level of dead or dying cells.
source: We found that newly eclosed flies exhibit a low level of dead or dying cells but from day 7 to day 56, the brain shows a relatively steady level (~5%) of dead or dying cells (Figure 6F) although there is variability from animal to animal.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: From day 7 to day 56, the brain shows a relatively steady level (~5%) of dead or dying cells.
source: We found that newly eclosed flies exhibit a low level of dead or dying cells but from day 7 to day 56, the brain shows a relatively steady level (~5%) of dead or dying cells (Figure 6F) although there is variability from animal to animal.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There is variability from animal to animal in the level of dead or dying cells.
source: We found that newly eclosed flies exhibit a low level of dead or dying cells but from day 7 to day 56, the brain shows a relatively steady level (~5%) of dead or dying cells (Figure 6F) although there is variability from animal to animal.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: This steady rate of cell death is expected to result in a predictable rate of cell loss in the brain with age.
source: Since dead cells are cleared in the brain (Kurant, 2011), we expect this steady rate of cell death to result in a predictable rate of cell loss in the brain with age, which closely agrees with our total cell counts performed using flow cytometry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell death measurements and citation to previous literature.

claim: The predictable rate of cell loss closely agrees with total cell counts performed using flow cytometry.
source: Since dead cells are cleared in the brain (Kurant, 2011), we expect this steady rate of cell death to result in a predictable rate of cell loss in the brain with age, which closely agrees with our total cell counts performed using flow cytometry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: While ~7% of the diploid cells incorporate PI, less than ~2.5% of polyploid cells incorporate PI in 2 week old Canton-S males.
source: We found that while ~7% of the diploid cells incorporate PI, less than ~2.5% of polyploid cells incorporate PI (Figure 6G), suggesting that polyploid cells are more resistant to cell death.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Polyploid cells are more resistant to cell death than diploid cells.
source: We found that while ~7% of the diploid cells incorporate PI, less than ~2.5% of polyploid cells incorporate PI (Figure 6G), suggesting that polyploid cells are more resistant to cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential PI incorporation between diploid and polyploid cells.

claim: High levels of PI incorporation are observed at 24 hr post exposure to 480mJ UV in 21 day old flies.
source: We observe high levels of PI incorporation (Figure 6H,I) at 24 hr post exposure, but normal levels by 48 hr, indicating an acute response of DNA damage induced cell death in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: Normal levels of PI incorporation are observed by 48 hr post UV exposure, indicating an acute response of DNA damage induced cell death in the brain.
source: We observe high levels of PI incorporation (Figure 6H,I) at 24 hr post exposure, but normal levels by 48 hr, indicating an acute response of DNA damage induced cell death in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: Many diploid cells die in response to 480mJ UV (~24.5%).
source: Many diploid cells die in response to this dose of UV (~24.5%).
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The polyploid cells show very low levels of PI incorporation (~3.1%) after 480mJ UV exposure.
source: In contrast, the polyploid cells show very low levels of PI incorporation (~3.1%, Figure 6H), suggesting that the polyploid cells in older adult brains are also resistant to DNA damage induced cell death.
evidence: This is supported by PI incorporation data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The polyploid cells in older adult brains are resistant to DNA damage induced cell death.
source: In contrast, the polyploid cells show very low levels of PI incorporation (~3.1%, Figure 6H), suggesting that the polyploid cells in older adult brains are also resistant to DNA damage induced cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low PI incorporation in polyploid cells after UV exposure.

claim: At 48 hr post UV exposure, an average 4% increase in polyploidy is observed for UV exposed animals.
source: We next examined whether the exposure to DNA damage also altered polyploidy, as we had observed in younger animals (Figure 6C). At 48 hr we observed, on average, a 4% increase in polyploidy for UV exposed animals.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The early increase in polyploidy at 48hr post UV exposure can be almost entirely attributed to the loss of the diploid cells that are PI positive at 24 hr post exposure.
source: This early increase can be almost entirely attributed to the loss of the diploid cells that are PI positive at 24 hr post exposure (a loss of 24.5% of diploid cells increases the proportion of polyploid cells from 18.9% to 23%).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculation of expected polyploidy increase from diploid cell loss.

claim: When comparing 48 hr to 5 days post UV exposure, there is no significant increase in polyploidy.
source: When comparing 48 hr to 5 days post exposure, we see no significant increase in polyploidy, suggesting that after 3 weeks of age, animals lose the ability to further increase polyploidy in response to damage.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: After 3 weeks of age, animals lose the ability to further increase polyploidy in response to damage.
source: When comparing 48 hr to 5 days post exposure, we see no significant increase in polyploidy, suggesting that after 3 weeks of age, animals lose the ability to further increase polyploidy in response to damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of polyploidy increase after UV exposure in older animals.

claim: Cells in the early adult fly brain undergo endoreplication and polyploidization in response to DNA damage and oxidative stress accumulated with age.
source: The work described in this study supports a model (Figure 6K) where cells in the early adult fly brain undergo endoreplication and polyploidization in response to DNA damage and oxidative stress accumulated with age.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Polyploid cells are more resistant to cell death and may serve a beneficial or neuroprotective role in the ageing brain.
source: Our data also suggest that polyploid cells are more resistant to cell death and may serve a beneficial or neuroprotective role in the ageing brain.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Polyploidy in neurons has previously been reported in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Polyploidy in neurons has previously been reported in the mouse cerebral cortex (López-Sánchez et al., 2017a; López-Sánchez and Frade, 2013) and chick retinal ganglion cells (Morillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidy in neurons has previously been reported in chick retinal ganglion cells.
source: Polyploidy in neurons has previously been reported in the mouse cerebral cortex (López-Sánchez et al., 2017a; López-Sánchez and Frade, 2013) and chick retinal ganglion cells (Morillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Whether purkinje cells in the mammalian cerebellum are polyploid has been a matter of considerable debate over the past several decades.
source: Whether purkinje cells in the mammalian cerebellum are polyploid has been a matter of considerable debate over the past several decades. (Brodskii et al., 1971; Del Monte, 2006; Kemp et al., 2012; Lapham, 1968; Lapham et al., 1971; Mares et al., 1973; Swartz and Bhatnagar, 1981).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Giant neurons in the terrestrial slug Limax contain >100,000 copies of the diploid genome.
source: Perhaps the most exaggerated examples of polyploidy are from the giant neurons in the terrestrial slug Limax (Yamagishi et al., 2011) and the sea slug Aplysia (Coggeshall et al., 1970) where giant neurons contain >100,000 copies of the diploid genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Giant neurons in the sea slug Aplysia contain >100,000 copies of the diploid genome.
source: Perhaps the most exaggerated examples of polyploidy are from the giant neurons in the terrestrial slug Limax (Yamagishi et al., 2011) and the sea slug Aplysia (Coggeshall et al., 1970) where giant neurons contain >100,000 copies of the diploid genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In all previously reported cases of neuronal polyploidy, polyploid neurons appear during development.
source: However, in all these cases, polyploid neurons appear during development.
evidence: This is a statement summarizing previous findings in the field.

claim: This study describes a novel phenomenon of adult onset and accumulation of polyploidy in the Drosophila brain under normal physiological ageing conditions.
source: Our study describes a novel phenomenon of adult onset and accumulation of polyploidy in the Drosophila brain under normal physiological ageing conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Polyploid intestinal enterocytes undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of cell-cell junctions in the epithelium.
source: In Drosophila, polyploid intestinal enterocytes (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018), SPGs (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2018) and cells in the wounded epithelium (Losick, 2016; Losick et al., 2013) undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of the blood brain barrier and the cell-cell junctions in the epithelium respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploid SPGs undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of the blood brain barrier.
source: In Drosophila, polyploid intestinal enterocytes (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018), SPGs (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2018) and cells in the wounded epithelium (Losick, 2016; Losick et al., 2013) undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of the blood brain barrier and the cell-cell junctions in the epithelium respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in the wounded epithelium undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of cell-cell junctions.
source: In Drosophila, polyploid intestinal enterocytes (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018), SPGs (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Von Stetina et al., 2018) and cells in the wounded epithelium (Losick, 2016; Losick et al., 2013) undergo endoreduplication and do not undergo cytokinesis to maintain the integrity of the blood brain barrier and the cell-cell junctions in the epithelium respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidy may allow cells to compensate for cell loss while maintaining established cell-cell contacts.
source: One possibility is that polyploidy in neurons or glia may allow cells to compensate for cell loss while maintaining established cell-cell contacts (Unhavaithaya and Orr-Weaver, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on previous findings and citation to literature.

claim: The compound eye and optic lobes of Drosophila contain ~750–800 ommatidial 'units' that form a highly organized and crystalline structure.
source: The compound eye and optic lobes of Drosophila contain ~750–800 ommatidial 'units' that form a highly organized and crystalline structure (Bates et al., 2019; Nériec and Desplan, 2016; Pecot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Numerically and topographically matched cells in the medulla cortex of the optic lobes receive inputs from the lamina which in turn receives inputs from the retina.
source: Numerically and topographically matched cells in the medulla cortex of the optic lobes receive inputs from the lamina which in turn receives inputs from the retina (Bates et al., 2019; Pecot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several cell types in the brain show a decline in number with age.
source: We observe polyploidization in multiple neuronal types found in the medulla, yet several cell types in the brain show a decline in number with age (Bates et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidy may allow neurons to form more presynaptic and postsynaptic connections to compensate for lost cells while maintaining the integrity of existing connections in the visual system.
source: It is possible that polyploidy allows neurons to form more presynaptic and postsynaptic connections to compensate for lost cells while maintaining the integrity of existing connections in the visual system.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the context and observations.

claim: In neurons, polyploidy could play a role in helping cells increase their soma size and dendritic arbors.
source: In neurons, polyploidy could play a role in helping cells increase their soma size and dendritic arbors (Morillo et al., 2010; Szaro and Tompkins, 1987).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nurse cells in the egg chamber become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
source: Nurse cells in the egg chamber (Lilly and Spradling, 1996; Wattiaux and Tsien, 1971), cells in the accessory gland (Box et al., 2019; Sitnik et al., 2016), salivary gland (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001) and fat body (Guarner et al., 2017), on the other hand become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in the accessory gland become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
source: Nurse cells in the egg chamber (Lilly and Spradling, 1996; Wattiaux and Tsien, 1971), cells in the accessory gland (Box et al., 2019; Sitnik et al., 2016), salivary gland (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001) and fat body (Guarner et al., 2017), on the other hand become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in the salivary gland become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
source: Nurse cells in the egg chamber (Lilly and Spradling, 1996; Wattiaux and Tsien, 1971), cells in the accessory gland (Box et al., 2019; Sitnik et al., 2016), salivary gland (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001) and fat body (Guarner et al., 2017), on the other hand become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in the fat body become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
source: Nurse cells in the egg chamber (Lilly and Spradling, 1996; Wattiaux and Tsien, 1971), cells in the accessory gland (Box et al., 2019; Sitnik et al., 2016), salivary gland (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001) and fat body (Guarner et al., 2017), on the other hand become polyploid to fulfill increased biosynthetic demands.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNAseq data suggest compromised metabolism with age in all parts of the brain.
source: In addition to an upregulation of DNA damage and cell cycle in the optic lobes, our RNAseq data suggest compromised metabolism with age in all parts of the brain.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: One of the main functions of glial cells is to provide metabolic support to neurons in the brain.
source: One of the main functions of glial cells is to provide metabolic support to neurons in the brain (Kremer et al., 2017; Schirmeier et al., 2016; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polyploidization in astrocyte and cortex glial cells might serve to increase their metabolic output and compensate for the reduced metabolic output in the ageing brain.
source: Polyploidization in astrocyte and cortex glial cells might also serve to increase their metabolic output and compensate for the reduced metabolic output in the ageing brain.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the context and observations.

claim: Signatures of ageing appear gradually over the course of an organism's lifespan and not abruptly at later chronological ages.
source: This is consistent with other studies that report that signatures of ageing appear gradually over the course of an organism's lifespan and not abruptly at later chronological ages (Ben-Zvi et al., 2009; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014; Shavlakadze et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Homology-directed repair of DNA lesions occurs in S and G2 phases of the cell cycle in actively dividing cells.
source: Homology-directed repair of DNA lesions occurs in S and G2 phases of the cell cycle in actively dividing cells (Herrup and Yang, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In other phases of the cell cycle, and after cell cycle exit, cells have to rely on error-prone non-homologous end joining mediated repair.
source: In other phases of the cell cycle, and after cell cycle exit, cells have to rely on error-prone non-homologous end joining mediated repair.
evidence: This is a statement reflecting established knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: Re-entering the cell cycle may allow postmitotic cells to repair DNA damage better and survive.
source: It is tempting to speculate that re-entering the cell cycle allows postmitotic cells to repair DNA damage better and survive.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the context and observations.

claim: A steady decline in the number of cells in the adult Drosophila brain with age is observed.
source: We and others observe a steady decline in the number of cells in the adult Drosophila brain with age (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Bates et al., 2019; Foo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous literature.

claim: The continual loss of cells in the ageing brain may be analogous to wounding, which induces polyploidization or compensatory cellular hypertrophy in other Drosophila tissues.
source: The continual loss of cells in the ageing brain may be analogous to wounding, which induces polyploidization or compensatory cellular hypertrophy in other Drosophila tissues (Bretscher and Fox, 2016; Cohen et al., 2018; Losick et al., 2013), (Tamori and Deng, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons and glia in the adult brain may employ a strategy similar to wounding-induced polyploidization to compensate for cell loss in a non-autonomous fashion.
source: We suggest neurons and glia in the adult brain may employ a similar strategy, to compensate for cell loss in a non-autonomous fashion.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observations and context.

claim: When damage is induced that does not increase cell death in young brains, an earlier increase in polyploidy is observed.
source: When we induce damage that does not increase cell death in young brains (Figure 6B,D) we observe an earlier increase in polyploidy, suggesting that in younger animals polyploidy can be an adaptive response to damage.
evidence: This is supported by paraquat treatment data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: In younger animals polyploidy can be an adaptive response to damage.
source: When we induce damage that does not increase cell death in young brains (Figure 6B,D) we observe an earlier increase in polyploidy, suggesting that in younger animals polyploidy can be an adaptive response to damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the paraquat treatment experiments.

claim: In older animals, polyploidy can protect from acute cell loss.
source: By contrast in older animals, we find that polyploidy can protect from acute cell loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the UV treatment experiments in aged animals.

claim: Levels of polyploidy do not further increase in aged animals after damage.
source: However, levels of subsequent polyploidy do not further increase in aged animals, suggesting there is a permissive window for damage-induced polyploidy during adulthood (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by UV treatment data in aged animals shown in Figure 6J.

claim: There is a permissive window for damage-induced polyploidy during adulthood.
source: However, levels of subsequent polyploidy do not further increase in aged animals, suggesting there is a permissive window for damage-induced polyploidy during adulthood (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that polyploidy increases in young but not old animals after damage.

claim: Levels of polyploidy plateau after 3–4 weeks of age in various strains.
source: This may explain why levels of polyploidy plateau after 3–4 weeks of age in various strains (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Over the past two decades, several studies have reported a correlation between neurodegeneration and cell cycle re-entry in neurons.
source: Over the past two decades, several studies have reported an interesting correlation between neurodegeneration and cell cycle re-entry in neurons (Chen et al., 2010; Frade and Ovejero-Benito, 2015; Herrup, 2012; Moh et al., 2011; Rimkus et al., 2008; Yang and Herrup, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most observations of cell cycle re-entry in neurodegeneration are from post-mortem brains containing neurons expressing cell cycle genes or exhibiting hyperploidy.
source: Most of these observations are from post-mortem brains containing neurons expressing cell cycle genes or exhibiting hyperploidy (>2N DNA content).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of previous observations in the field.

claim: More hyperploidy is observed in brains of patients with preclinical Alzheimer's compared to age-matched controls.
source: More hyperploidy is observed in brains of patients with preclinical Alzheimer's compared to age-matched controls, which has led to the hypothesis that cell cycle re-entry may precede cell death and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the field.

claim: The hypothesis that cell cycle re-entry may precede cell death and neurodegeneration has been proposed.
source: More hyperploidy is observed in brains of patients with preclinical Alzheimer's compared to age-matched controls, which has led to the hypothesis that cell cycle re-entry may precede cell death and neurodegeneration.
